figures.alt: Photo of wind-bent beach grass on a rippled sand dune under a blue sky.
figures.caption: Wind moves sand a little at a time. Grass roots hold it in place.

figures.alt: Photo of layered tan sandstone cliffs with rust-orange and green-gray streaks running down the rock, above dark blue lake water, with pines on top.
figures.caption: Water and ice have worn these cliffs over a very long time. Some changes are slow.

figures.alt: Photo of a plastic tray holding a sand slope, a patch of grass on one side, a few stones on the other and a small cup of water.
figures.caption: The Erosion Guard tray before the test: sand, two guards (grass and stones) and water to pour.

figures.alt: Illustration of three students at a classroom table with a sand erosion tray: a girl pours water from a cup, a boy checks the sand with his finger and a third student writes down the result.
figures.caption: Teams share the jobs in the Erosion Guard test: pour the same amount each time, measure the sand that moved, and record it.

figures.alt: Interactive: wind blows over a sand mound with or without grass and counts how many grains move.
figures.caption: Blow wind over bare sand and over sand with grass.

figures.alt: Grouped bar graph of sand moved in finger widths over 3 tries. No guard: 4, 5, 4. Grass: 1, 1, 2. Stones: 2, 1, 2. Paper barrier: 3, 3, 2.
figures.caption: Sand moved in 3 tries for each guard. Grass moved the least sand. With no guard the sand moved 4 to 5 finger widths.
